The Claude Code Setup Nobody Talks About: From Solo Agent to Full Dev Team

Bokiko
15 min read
·
Mar 10, 2026

Most developers install Claude Code, type a question, get an answer, and think that’s the product. They’re using maybe 10% of what it can do.

I know because I was one of them. For months, I treated Claude Code like a fancy autocomplete — ask a question, paste the answer, move on. Then I spent a weekend actually configuring it. I added skills, installed plugins, set up custom subagents, and experimented with agent teams. The difference wasn’t incremental. It was like going from a calculator to a spreadsheet.

An unconfigured Claude Code is a single developer who’s smart but has amnesia. A configured one is a team of specialists who know your codebase, follow your conventions, and execute multi-step workflows without being told twice.

This article covers the four extension layers that make that possible: skills, plugins, subagents, and agent teams. What each one is, when to use which, and how to set them up — with real examples you can copy and paste today.

Whether you’re new to Claude Code or you’ve been using it for months, there’s almost certainly a layer here you haven’t touched.

The Hierarchy: Understanding What’s What

Before we configure anything, let’s get the mental model right. Claude Code has four extension mechanisms, and they serve very different purposes:

Extension What It Is Analogy When to Use Skills Markdown playbooks that teach Claude workflows A checklist a new hire follows Repeatable tasks, conventions, deployment steps Plugins Packaged bundles of skills + agents + hooks An app from the app store Team-wide tooling, community extensions, LSP support Subagents Isolated AI workers with their own context A contractor you hand a task to Heavy research, code review, isolated implementation Agent Teams Multiple Claude instances coordinating together A whole project team Parallel review, competing hypotheses, cross-layer changes

The key insight: these stack. You don’t choose one. You layer them. Skills teach Claude how to work. Plugins give it tools. Subagents give it workers. Agent teams give it a crew.

Here’s a decision tree:

  • “Claude should always do X this way” → Skill
  • “I want this tool/integration available” → Plugin
  • “Do this task without polluting my conversation” → Subagent
  • “Work on multiple things in parallel and coordinate” → Agent Team

Now let’s dig into each one.

Skills: Teaching Claude HOW to Work

A skill is a markdown file that gives Claude a playbook. Instead of re-explaining your deployment process or code review checklist every session, you write it once as a SKILL.md file, and Claude uses it whenever it's relevant — or you invoke it directly with /skill-name.

Where Skills Live

Location Path Who Can Use It Enterprise Via managed settings All users in your organization Personal ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md You, across all projects Project .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md Anyone on this project Plugin <plugin>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md Wherever the plugin is enabled

When skills share the same name across levels, higher-priority locations win: enterprise > personal > project. Plugin skills use a plugin-name:skill-name namespace, so they never conflict.

What a Skill Looks Like

Here’s a deploy skill that only you can trigger (Claude won’t run it automatically):

---
name: deploy
description: Deploy the application to production
disable-model-invocation: true
---
Deploy $ARGUMENTS to production:1. Run the full test suite — abort if anything fails
2. Build the production bundle
3. Push to the deployment target
4. Run a smoke test against the live URL
5. Post a summary of what was deployed

Now instead of typing four paragraphs explaining your deploy process, you type:

/deploy staging

Done.

Two Types of Skills

Reference skills add persistent knowledge. Think coding conventions, API patterns, domain context. Claude loads these automatically when they’re relevant:

---
name: api-conventions
description: REST API design patterns for this codebase
---
When writing API endpoints:
- Use RESTful naming: plural nouns, no verbs in URLs
- Return consistent error format: { error: string, code: number }
- Always validate request bodies with Zod/Pydantic
- Include pagination for list endpoints (cursor-based, not offset)

Task skills are step-by-step workflows you invoke on demand. Add disable-model-invocation: true so Claude doesn't trigger them on its own:

---
name: fix-issue
description: Fix a GitHub issue end-to-end
disable-model-invocation: true
---
Fix GitHub issue $ARGUMENTS:1. Fetch the issue description with `gh issue view $ARGUMENTS`
2. Understand the requirements and acceptance criteria
3. Find the relevant code
4. Implement the fix
5. Write tests covering the fix
6. Create a commit following conventional commit format

Advanced: Dynamic Context Injection

Skills can run shell commands before they reach Claude using the !`command` syntax:

---
name: pr-summary
description: Summarize the current pull request
context: fork
agent: Explore
---
## PR Context
- Diff: !`gh pr diff`
- Comments: !`gh pr view --comments`
- Changed files: !`gh pr diff --name-only`Summarize this pull request. Focus on what changed, why, and any risks.

The commands execute first, their output gets injected, and Claude only sees the result. This is preprocessing, not something Claude runs.

Claude Code skills follow the Agent Skills open standard — adopted by 26+ tools including Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Roo Code, and others. Write a skill once, use it across any compatible agent.

Bundled Skills You Already Have

Claude Code ships with powerful bundled skills that most developers never discover:

  • /simplify — Reviews your recently changed files for code reuse, quality, and efficiency issues, then fixes them. It spawns three review agents in parallel. Run it after implementing any feature.
  • /batch <instruction> — Orchestrates large-scale changes across a codebase in parallel. It researches the codebase, decomposes work into 5–30 independent units, and spawns one background agent per unit — each in an isolated git worktree. Example: /batch migrate src/ from Solid to React.
  • /loop [interval] <prompt> — Runs a prompt repeatedly on an interval. Useful for polling deployments or babysitting PRs. Example: /loop 5m check if the deploy finished.
  • /claude-api — Loads Claude API reference material for your project's language. Also activates automatically when your code imports Anthropic SDKs.

The Bold Take

If you don’t have at least 5 custom skills, you’re doing manual labor the AI should handle. Every time you find yourself typing the same instructions twice, that’s a skill waiting to be written. It takes 5 minutes to create one. It saves hours over weeks.

Plugins: The Game-Changer Nobody Installed Yet

Skills are individual playbooks. Plugins are packages — bundles of skills, subagents, hooks, MCP servers, and even LSP configurations, distributed through marketplaces and installable in three commands.

What Plugins Are

A plugin is a directory with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest and any combination of:

  • skills/ — Skills with SKILL.md files
  • agents/ — Custom subagent definitions
  • hooks/ — Event-driven automation (run linter after every file edit, etc.)
  • .mcp.json — MCP server configurations for external integrations
  • .lsp.json — Language server configurations for code intelligence

Plugin skills are namespaced (e.g., /commit-commands:commit) so they never conflict with your personal skills or other plugins.

The Official Marketplace

Claude Code ships with Anthropic’s official marketplace (claude-plugins-official) already available. Browse it with:

/plugin

Navigate to the Discover tab. Install anything directly:

/plugin install pyright-lsp@claude-plugins-official

Community Marketplaces

Anyone can create a marketplace. Add one from GitHub:

/plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-code

Or from any Git host:

/plugin marketplace add https://gitlab.com/your-team/claude-plugins.git

Top Plugins Worth Installing

Here are the plugins I’d install on any dev machine. The LSP and workflow plugins below are from the official Anthropic-managed marketplace (claude-plugins-official). Some external integration plugins may be available through community marketplaces — always verify the source before installing.

⚠️ Security note: Plugins can include executable code in skills and hooks. Always review a plugin’s source code before installing, especially from community marketplaces. Only install plugins from sources you trust.

Code Intelligence (from the official marketplace — pick your language):

Language Plugin What It Does TypeScript typescript-lsp Type errors after every edit, jump-to-definition, find references Python pyright-lsp Same — type checking, diagnostics, navigation Rust rust-analyzer-lsp Full Rust language intelligence Go gopls-lsp Go language server support C/C++ clangd-lsp Clang-based code intelligence Java jdtls-lsp Eclipse JDT language server Kotlin kotlin-lsp Kotlin language support Swift swift-lsp Swift language support C# csharp-lsp C# language intelligence PHP php-lsp PHP language support Lua lua-lsp Lua language support

Once installed, Claude gets automatic diagnostics — after every file edit, the language server analyzes changes and reports type errors, missing imports, and syntax issues. Claude sees and fixes problems in the same turn, without running a compiler. This alone is worth the install.

External Integrations (availability varies — check the official and community marketplaces):

Plugin What It Does github PR reviews, issue management, repo operations gitlab GitLab project management and CI/CD linear Project management directly from Claude slack Read and send messages without leaving your terminal playwright Browser automation and testing

Development Workflows (from the official marketplace):

Plugin What It Does commit-commands Git commit workflows: stage, message, push, PR — one command security-guidance Security best practices and vulnerability checking plugin-dev Toolkit for creating your own plugins skill-creator Guided skill creation workflow

Team Plugins

For teams, you can configure automatic marketplace installation in .claude/settings.json:

{
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "my-team-tools": {
      "source": {
        "source": "github",
        "repo": "your-org/claude-plugins"
      }
    }
  }
}

When team members trust the project, they get prompted to install your marketplace and plugins automatically. Zero manual setup for new developers.

The Bold Take

An unconfigured Claude Code is like a smartphone with zero apps. The hardware is impressive, but you’re not using it for anything it’s actually good at. Install a few plugins. It takes 2 minutes. The productivity difference is immediate.

Subagents: Delegation That Actually Works

Here’s the problem with doing everything in one conversation: context fills up. You ask Claude to research a codebase, it reads 40 files, and now your conversation is stuffed with exploration noise. Your actual implementation request gets worse answers because the important context is buried under search results.

Subagents fix this. A subagent is an isolated Claude instance with its own context window, system prompt, and tool access. It does its job, returns a summary, and your main conversation stays clean.

Built-in Subagents

Claude Code ships with several built-in subagents. The three you’ll interact with most:

  • Explore — Fast, read-only (runs on Haiku). Used for file discovery and codebase search. Claude specifies a thoroughness level: quick, medium, or very thorough.
  • Plan — Read-only researcher for plan mode. Gathers context before presenting plans.
  • General-purpose — Full tool access. For complex, multi-step tasks.

Additional helper agents handle specific tasks behind the scenes (Bash execution, statusline setup, Claude Code Guide for feature questions).

Claude delegates to these automatically. When you ask “How does the auth module work?”, it spawns an Explore subagent to investigate, gets a summary, and responds — without filling your conversation with 30 file reads.

Custom Subagents

This is where it gets powerful. You can create subagents interactively with the /agents command (which can even generate the config with Claude), or manually create a Markdown file in .claude/agents/ (project-level) or ~/.claude/agents/ (personal):

---
name: db-optimizer
description: PostgreSQL performance specialist. Use when optimizing queries, analyzing EXPLAIN output, or improving database schema.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---
You are a PostgreSQL performance expert. When asked to optimize:1. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the target query
2. Identify missing indexes, sequential scans, and join inefficiencies
3. Propose specific changes with expected performance impact
4. Generate migration files for any schema changes
5. Verify improvements with before/after benchmarksAlways consider the impact on write performance when adding indexes.

Now when you say “optimize the user search query,” Claude delegates to your db-optimizer with all the right context and constraints.

Key Benefits

Context preservation. The main conversation stays focused. Subagent output gets summarized before returning.

Tool restrictions. A code reviewer subagent can be limited to read-only tools — Read, Grep, Glob — so it literally cannot modify your code.

Model selection. Route simple tasks to Haiku (fast, cheap) and complex tasks to Opus (powerful). A code review subagent on Sonnet gives you 90% of the quality at a fraction of the cost.

Persistent memory. Add memory: user to your subagent config and it builds up knowledge across sessions. Three scopes are available:

Scope Location Use When user ~/.claude/agent-memory/<name>/ Learnings should apply across all projects project .claude/agent-memory/<name>/ Knowledge is project-specific and shareable via version control local .claude/agent-memory-local/<name>/ Project-specific but should not be checked in

---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices
memory: user
---
You are a senior code reviewer. As you review code, update your agent
memory with patterns, conventions, and recurring issues you discover.

Over time, the reviewer learns your team’s patterns and gets better.

Worktree isolation. Add isolation: worktree to run a subagent in a temporary git worktree — an isolated copy of the repository. The worktree is automatically cleaned up if the subagent makes no changes. This is essential for parallel work where multiple subagents might edit overlapping files.

Foreground vs. Background

Subagents can run in the foreground (blocking — you wait for results) or background (concurrent — you keep working). Press Ctrl+B to background a running subagent. Use Ctrl+F to kill all background agents if needed.

Use background subagents for tasks that don’t block your next step — running a test suite, doing a code review, or generating documentation while you keep coding.

The Bold Take

Every time you read more than 3 files to understand something, you should be using a subagent. Your main context window is precious real estate. Don’t waste it on exploration. Delegate, get the summary, and use that context for the work that matters.

Agent Teams: The Experimental Nuclear Option

Subagents are workers that report back to you. Agent teams are crews that coordinate with each other.

An agent team consists of a lead (your main session) and multiple teammates (independent Claude instances). Each teammate has its own context window and can:

  • Claim tasks from a shared task list
  • Send messages to other teammates directly
  • Work in parallel on different parts of a problem

This is fundamentally different from subagents. Subagents can only report back to the parent — they can’t communicate with each other. Agent teams remove that bottleneck entirely with lateral messaging and a shared task board.

How to Enable

Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default. Enable them in your settings.json:

{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1"
  }
}

Two display modes are available:

  • In-process (default): all teammates run in your terminal. Use Shift+Down to cycle through them. Works everywhere.
  • Split panes: each teammate gets its own pane via tmux or iTerm2. Set "teammateMode": "tmux" in settings.

You can also require plan approval for teammates — they work in read-only mode until the lead approves their approach, which is useful for risky refactors.

When Agent Teams Shine

Parallel code review with different lenses:

Create an agent team to review PR #142. Spawn three reviewers:
- One focused on security implications
- One checking performance impact
- One validating test coverage
Have them each review and report findings.

Each reviewer works independently with a different focus. The lead synthesizes findings.

Debugging with competing hypotheses:

Users report the WebSocket disconnects after one message.
Spawn 4 teammates to investigate different theories. Have them
debate each other — try to disprove each other's hypotheses.
Update findings with whatever consensus emerges.

The adversarial structure fights anchoring bias. Instead of one agent finding a plausible explanation and stopping, four agents actively try to break each other’s theories. The surviving hypothesis is much more likely to be correct.

Cross-layer implementation:

Create a team to implement the new notification feature:
- Frontend teammate: React components and state management
- Backend teammate: API endpoints and database schema
- Test teammate: Integration and unit tests
Each owns their layer. Coordinate through the shared task list.

The Honest Take

Agent teams are powerful but expensive. Each teammate is a separate Claude instance with its own context window. Token usage scales linearly with team size. Use them for big tasks where parallel exploration genuinely adds value — research, review, cross-layer changes, competing hypotheses.

For routine work, a single session with subagents is more cost-effective. Start with 3–5 teammates. More than that and coordination overhead outweighs the benefit.

And a practical note: agent teams are still experimental. Known limitations from the official docs:

  • Session resumption (/resume) doesn't restore in-process teammates
  • Task status can lag — teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks complete
  • Shutdown can be slow (teammates finish their current request first)
  • One team per session, no nested teams, lead can’t be transferred
  • Split panes require tmux or iTerm2 (not available in all terminal emulators)

They’re incredible when they work, but set expectations accordingly.

The Setup That Actually Works

Here’s the step-by-step to go from default Claude Code to a fully configured setup.

Step 1: Install Core Plugins (2 minutes)

Open Claude Code and run /plugin to browse the official marketplace, or install directly:

/plugin install typescript-lsp@claude-plugins-official
/plugin install github@claude-plugins-official
/plugin install commit-commands@claude-plugins-official
/plugin install security-guidance@claude-plugins-official

Swap typescript-lsp for your language's LSP plugin (11 languages available in the official marketplace). The github plugin gives you PR and issue management. commit-commands handles the git workflow. security-guidance adds security best practices.

Before installing any plugin, take a moment to review what it includes. Plugins can contain hooks that execute code automatically on events like file saves. Stick to the official marketplace for maximum trust, and review community plugins before enabling them.

Step 2: Create Your First 3 Skills (10 minutes)

A commit skill:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/commit && cat > ~/.claude/skills/commit/SKILL.md << 'EOF'
---
name: commit
description: Create a well-formatted git commit
disable-model-invocation: true
---
Create a git commit for the current changes:
1. Run `git diff --staged` to see what's staged
2. If nothing is staged, stage the relevant files (never use `git add .`)
3. Write a conventional commit message (feat:, fix:, docs:, etc.)
4. Focus on WHY, not WHAT
5. Create the commit
EOF

A review skill:

mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills/review && cat > ~/.claude/skills/review/SKILL.md << 'EOF'
---
name: review
description: Review recent code changes for quality issues
context: fork
agent: Explore
---
Review the most recent changes in this repository:
1. Run `git diff HEAD~1` to see what changed
2. Check for: security issues, performance problems, missing error handling
3. Verify naming conventions and code style
4. Look for missing tests
5. Provide specific, actionable feedback organized by severity
EOF

A project conventions skill (auto-loaded):

mkdir -p .claude/skills/conventions && cat > .claude/skills/conventions/SKILL.md << 'EOF'
---
name: conventions
description: Project coding conventions and patterns. Use when writing or reviewing code.
---
## Code Conventions
- Use TypeScript strict mode
- Error handling: always use Result types, never throw
- API responses: { data: T } on success, { error: string, code: number } on failure
- Tests: colocate with source files as *.test.ts
- Imports: use path aliases (@/components, @/utils)
EOF

Step 3: Create a Custom Subagent (5 minutes)

mkdir -p ~/.claude/agents && cat > ~/.claude/agents/researcher.md << 'EOF'
---
name: researcher
description: Deep codebase researcher. Use when exploring unfamiliar code, understanding architecture, or mapping dependencies.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: sonnet
---
You are a codebase researcher. When asked to investigate:1. Start with the directory structure to understand project layout
2. Identify entry points and key modules
3. Trace data flow through the system
4. Map dependencies between components
5. Return a clear summary with file referencesBe thorough but concise. Include file paths for every claim.
EOF

Recommended Stack by Developer Type

Frontend / React:

  • Plugins: typescript-lsp, github, commit-commands
  • Skills: component generator, styling conventions, accessibility checker
  • Subagent: design-system reviewer (enforces component library usage)

Backend / API:

  • Plugins: pyright-lsp or gopls-lsp, github, security-guidance
  • Skills: endpoint scaffolder, migration generator, API conventions
  • Subagent: query optimizer, security auditor

Full-Stack:

  • All of the above, plus a researcher subagent for codebase exploration workflows

DevOps / Platform:

  • Plugins: github or gitlab, playwright
  • Skills: deploy workflow, incident response playbook, infrastructure conventions
  • Subagent: config validator (read-only, checks IaC for issues)

The Real Advantage

The gap between a default Claude Code installation and a configured one isn’t a marginal improvement. It’s a fundamentally different tool.

Default Claude Code is one generalist who forgets everything between sessions. Configured Claude Code is a team of specialists who know your conventions, follow your workflows, and preserve context across conversations. Skills encode your team’s knowledge so it never has to be explained twice. Plugins connect Claude to your actual development tools. Subagents keep your context clean and let you delegate without micromanaging. Agent teams unlock genuine parallelism for the tasks that need it.

This isn’t about AI replacing developers. It’s about AI that knows your workflow — your deployment process, your code conventions, your review checklist, your database optimization patterns. That’s what skills and subagents encode: institutional knowledge that scales.

Start small. Install a few plugins. Write your first skill. Create one custom subagent. Use them for a week. Then come back and build from there.

The developers who figure this out early won’t just be faster. They’ll be operating on a different level entirely.

All examples in this article use Claude Code v2.1.x (current as of March 2026). Skills, plugins, and subagents are stable features. Agent teams are experimental and require opt-in. LSP plugins are from the official Anthropic-managed marketplace — always verify plugin sources before installing. For the latest documentation, visit code.claude.com/docs.
